Verses of Dhamma
Chapter of Pairs
All things are preceded by the mind,  surpassed by the mind, created by the mind.  If one speaks or acts  with a corrupted mind,  Then suffering follows,  As a track follows a wheel.
All things are preceded by the mind,  surpassed by the mind, created by the mind.  If one speaks or acts  with a pure mind,  Then happiness follows,  As a shadow that never leaves.
“They abused me, they hurt me,  they defeated me, they robbed me!”  For those who hold on to this  hostility is never replaced by peace.
“They abused me, they hurt me,  they defeated me, they robbed me!”  For those who do not hold on to this  hostility is replaced by peace.
Hostility is never pacified  by means of hostility.  Only by means of non-hostility is it pacified.  This is an eternal truth.
Others do not know  that we must be restrained.  The wise ones who know this  attain peace.
If one focuses on beauty,  lacks sense-restraint,  does not know the right amount when eating,  is lazy, and lacks energy,  Māra subdues such a person  just as the wind subdues a weak tree.

If one does not focus on beauty,  has good sense-restraint,  knows the right amount when eating,  has faith, and has persistent energy,  Māra does not subdue such a person  just as the wind does not subdue a stone mountain.
An impure person  who dons a monastic robe  without true self-control  is not worthy of the monastic robe.
One who has expelled all impurity,  is focused on moral conduct,  and is committed to true self-control  is worthy of the monastic robe.
One who thinks the non-essential is essential  and who sees the essential as non-essential  does not arrive at the essence;  their conduct is based on incorrect attitudes.
One who knows the essential as essential  and the non-essential as non-essential  arrives at the essence;  their conduct is based on correct attitudes.
Just as rain penetrates  a poorly sealed house,  in the same way, passion penetrates  an undeveloped mind.
Just as rain does not penetrate  a well-sealed house,  in the same way, passion does not penetrate  a well-developed mind.
One sorrows here, one sorrows afterwards,  an evildoer sorrows both times.  One sorrows and agonizes  after seeing one's own defiled actions.
One rejoices here, one rejoices afterwards,  one who has made merit rejoices both times.  One rejoices and exults  after seeing one's own pure actions.
Tormented here, tormented afterwards,  an evildoer is tormented both times.  One is tormented by the thought “I have done evil,”  And one is tormented even more when one has arrived at a bad destiny.

One delights here, one delights afterwards,  one who has made merit delights both times.  One is delighted by the thought “I have made merit,”  And one delights even more when one has arrived at a good destiny.
A negligent person who says much that is beneficial  but does not act accordingly  is like a cowherd who counts other people's cows,  and is not part of the contemplative life.

Even if they say little that is beneficial,  one who lives according to the Dhamma,  having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion,  with accurate understanding and a well-liberated mind,  not grasping either here or beyond,  is part of the contemplative life.

Chapter on Non-Negligence
Non-negligence is the path of the Deathless,  negligence is the path of death.  Those who are not negligent never die,  those who are negligent are like the dead.
This is what the wise distinctly know  about non-negligence.  They rejoice in non-negligence,  enjoying the territory of the noble ones.
Those who meditate continuously,  who always persevere,  Steadfast, they touch Nibbāna— the unsurpassable safety.
Glory increases for those who are proactive and mindful,  with pure and careful conduct,  self-restrained, living the Dhamma,  and not negligent.
By being proactive and not negligent,  self-restrained and self-controlled,  a wise person makes an island  which no flood can submerge.
Fools and idiots commit  to negligence,  whereas a wise person protects non-negligence  as the greatest wealth.
Do not commit to negligence  or to involvement in sensuality;  for one who meditates without negligence  attains abundant bliss.

When a wise person dispels negligence  by practicing non-negligence,  then having ascended in the palace of wisdom,  sorrowless, they look at this sorrowful generation,  as a wise person on a mountain  looks down at the fools on the ground.
Not negligent amidst the negligent,  wide awake amidst the sleeping— like a swift horse leaving behind a feeble one,  the wise leave them behind and move on.
By means of non-negligence  Maghavā became the best of the angels;  they praise non-negligence,  whereas negligence is always criticized.
A monk who approves of non-negligence  and sees the danger in negligence  proceeds like a fire— burning up fetters, small and large.
A monk who approves of non-negligence  and sees the danger in negligence  cannot decline  and is close to Nibbāna.

Chapter on Mind
Unstable and unsteady is the mind,  difficult to protect and restrain.  The wise straighten it,  like a fletcher straightens an arrow.
Like a fish pulled from its home  and thrown on dry land,  the mind thrashes about,  struggling to escape the realm of Māra.
The mind is fast-moving and hard to subdue,  landing wherever it wishes;  it is good to train it— a trained mind brings happiness.
The mind is very subtle and hard to see,  landing wherever it wishes;  the wise protect it— a guarded mind brings happiness.
The mind travels far, wanders alone,  incorporeal, self-sheltered;  those who restrain it  become free from the bonds of Māra.
For one whose mind is unsettled,  who does not understand the true Dhamma,  and whose clarity is disturbed,  wisdom does not become complete.
One whose mind is free from influences,  whose mind is unafflicted,  who has abandoned both merit and evil, and is alert  has no fear.
Having understood that this body is like a clay pot,  having fortified the mind like a city,  combat Māra using wisdom as one's weapon,  and protect the victory—you can be free of any abode.
Before long, this body  will lie on the ground  discarded and devoid of consciousness  like a useless log.
Compared to what might be done by an enemy to an enemy  or one hostile person to another,  a wrongly directed mind  can cause even more harm than that.
Compared to what might be done by a mother or a father  or any other relative,  a rightly directed mind  can bring even more benefit than that.

Chapter on Flowers
Who will investigate this earth,  this world of death and angels?  Who will collect the well-taught verses of truth,  as a skilled florist collects flowers?
A trainee will investigate this earth,  this world of death and angels.  A trainee will collect the well-taught verses of truth,  as a skilled florist collects flowers.
Having understood that this body is like foam,  one who is aware that it is like a mirage,  having cut Māra’s flower strands,  goes where the Lord of Death does not see.
As if they were collecting flowers,  a person collects mental attachments;  like a sleeping village taken away by a great flood,  they are taken away by death.
As if they were collecting flowers,  a person collects mental attachments;  never sated when it comes to sensuality,  they are dominated by the Ender.
Just as a bee  takes nectar from a flower  without harming its beauty or fragrance— a sage behaves the same way when in a village.
Do not look at the faults of others— what they have or have not done;  Look only at yourself— what you have or have not done.
Just like a lovely flower  that has beauty but no fragrance,  well-spoken words  are fruitless when not acted out.
Just like a lovely flower  that has both beauty and fragrance,  well-spoken words  are fruitful when acted out.
Just as one might make many garlands  from a heap of flowers,  in the same way, between birth and death  one can do much that is wholesome.

The fragrance of a flower does not go against the wind;  nor does the fragrance of sandalwood, milkwood, or jasmine.  However, the fragrance of goodness does go against the wind;  a good person diffuses it in all directions.
Sandalwood or milkwood,  lotus or jasmine,  compared to these kinds of fragrances,  the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
The fragrance of milkwood and sandalwood  is insignificant;  the fragrance of virtue is the highest— it drifts amidst the angels.
The path of those who have perfect virtue,  live without negligence,  and are liberated through right knowledge  cannot be found by Māra.
Just as in a trash-heap  discarded by the side of the road,  a lotus might bloom— of pure fragrance and delightful to the mind—
in the same way, amidst the trash-heap of beings— the blind commoners— a disciple of the Completely Awakened One  outshines them with wisdom.

Chapter on Fools
Long is the night for one who is awake,  long is a yojana for one who is weary,  long is saṁsāra for fools  who do not understand the true Dhamma.
If you do not find a traveler  who is superior or equal to yourself,  then resolutely travel alone;  one cannot go with a fool.
A fool is tormented  by thoughts of children and wealth;  but since one does not even possess oneself,  how could one possess children and wealth?
A fool who conceives of foolishness  is wise in that regard;  but a fool who has the conceit of wisdom  can truly be called a fool.
Even if a fool spends a lifetime  in the presence of the wise,  they do not understand the Dhamma,  just as a spoon does not understand the flavor of soup.
Even if a discerning person spends only a moment  in the presence of the wise,  they quickly understand the Dhamma,  just as a tongue understands the flavor of soup.
Unwise fools act as if  they are not even their own friends— they perform evil actions  which yield bitter fruit.
It is not good to perform an action  which one will later regret,  when, weeping with a tearful face,  one experiences its result.
But it is good to perform an action  which one will not later regret,  when, satisfied and uplifted,  one experiences its result.
A fool thinks that evil is sweet  as long as its results have yet to fully manifest;  but when the results of that evil fully manifest,  then they descend into suffering.
Month after month  a fool might eat using the tip of a blade of grass;  but such a one is not worth even a sixteenth as much  as those who comprehend the Dhamma.
Once an evil action has been performed,  it is not released suddenly like milk;  burning, it follows a fool,  like fire concealed by ash.
It brings no benefit  when fame comes to a fool;  it destroys their good traits  and tears apart their head.
A fool wishes for a false existence— preeminence among monks,  dominion in residences,  and honor among other families.

“May both renunciants and laypeople  think it was done by me alone;  may I alone have the highest authority,  in determining what should or should not be done.”  In this way,  the attitude, desire, and conceit of a fool grows.

Knowledge is the cause of gain,  knowledge leads to Nibbāna;  since this is exactly what  a monastic disciple of the Buddha understands,  they do not delight in acclaim;  they devote themselves to seclusion.

Chapter on the Wise

Like a person who leads you to hidden treasure:  this is how to see a person who points out your faults.  A wise person who tells you what you need to subdue  is the kind of person you should associate with.  Associating with that kind of person  is always for the better and never for the worse.
A person might advise you, instruct you,  and keep you away from what is not good;  They are liked by those who are good,  and not liked by those who are not good.
Do not associate with evil friends,  do not associate with lowly people;  associate with good spiritual friends  and with the highest of people.
When one enjoys the Dhamma, then one sleeps happily,  with a clear mind;  a wise person always appreciates  the Dhamma proclaimed by the noble ones.
Irrigators guide water,  fletchers shape arrows,  carpenters shape wood,  the wise train themselves.
Just as the wind  does not move solid stone,  praise and criticism  do not disturb the wise.
Like a deep lake,  clear and undisturbed,  when the wise hear the Dhamma  they attain clarity.
Good people let go of everything;  the peaceful do not prattle about sensuality.  Whether they are touched by pleasure or pain,  neither elation nor depression can be seen in the wise.

Whether because of oneself or because of another,  one should not wish to obtain children, wealth, lordship, or personal success  in ways contrary to Dhamma.  Instead let one be virtuous, wise, and in accord with Dhamma.
Few are the humans  who go beyond.  Most people  only run around on the shore.
Those who act in accordance  with the well-explained Dhamma  will go beyond the mortal realm  so difficult to escape.
Abandon dark things and develop bright things;  a wise person  leaves home for homelessness  and lives in seclusion, where it is difficult to find satisfaction.
One who has nothing could hope to find satisfaction there,  after abandoning sensuality;  a wise person would cleanse themselves  of mental defilements.

Those who have developed the factors of awakening  correctly and thoroughly,  who have taken up relinquishment,  who appreciate non-grasping,  and have eliminated their corruptions— such radiant beings have attained Nibbāna in this world.

Chapter on Arahants
In one who has completed the journey, is free of sorrow,  has been completely liberated in every way,  and has abandoned all ties,  no fever can be found.
Mindfully they strive upwards,  they do not appreciate settling;  Like swans leaving behind a lake,  they abandon home after home.
Those who have no stockpile,  who have completely understood eating,  whose domain is emptiness  and objectless liberation— like birds in the sky,  their movement is hard to follow.
One who has completely eliminated their influences  and is not dependent on consumption,  whose domain is emptiness  and objectless liberation— like birds in the sky,  their path is hard to follow.
One whose faculties are peaceful,  like a horse well-trained by a charioteer,  who has abandoned conceit and is free of influences,  is envied even by the angels.
One who, like the earth, opposes nothing,  who is as stable as a pillar, practicing well,  who is like a lake with no trace of mud— such beings are not reborn in saṁsāra.
One whose mind is peaceful,  whose speech and actions are peaceful,  and who is liberated through right knowledge— such a person is at peace.
One who is beyond faith, knows the Unmade,  has severed all ties,  has expelled defilement, and has rejected longing— this is truly the best person.
Whether it is in a village or in the wilderness,  in lowlands or highlands— any place where an arahant lives  is a place worth appreciating.
It is possible to appreciate the wilderness areas  that most people do not appreciate;  one who is free of passion will appreciate them,  since they do not seek sensuality.

Chapter of Thousands
Rather than a thousand sayings  not connected to the goal,  it is better to have just one sentence about the goal  if one reaches peace after hearing it.
Rather than a thousand poems  not connected to the goal,  it is better to have just one line of a poem  if one reaches peace after hearing it.
One might utter a hundred poems  not connected to the goal;  it is better to have just one line of Dhamma  if one reaches peace after hearing it.
One might subjugate a million people  in battle,  but one who subjugates oneself  has won the ultimate victory.
It is better to subjugate yourself  than other people,  for one who is self-trained  always acts with restraint.
No angel or fairy,  demon or god,  can turn such a person’s  victory into defeat.

Every month one might conduct  a hundred sacrifices worth thousands;  Or for a single moment  one could pay homage to a self-developed person.  That homage is better  than a hundred years of sacrifices.
One might spend a hundred years  tending to a fire in a forest;  or for a single moment  one could pay homage to a self-developed person.  That homage is better  than a hundred years of sacrifices.
One could make any kind of offering or sacrifice in the world  for a year, pursuing merit;  but all of that is not even a quarter as good  as honoring those who are upright.
For one who is virtuous, respectful,  and always reverential towards the elderly,  four things increase:  vitality, beauty, pleasure, and strength.
Better than living for a hundred years  without virtue and concentration,  is living for one day  as a virtuous meditator.
Better than living for a hundred years  without wisdom and concentration,  is living for one day  as a wise meditator.
Better than living for a hundred years  with laziness and indolence,  is living for one day  with determination and resolve.
Better than living for a hundred years  without seeing arising and vanishing,  is living for one day  while seeing arising and vanishing.
Better than living for a hundred years  without seeing the path to the deathless,  is living for one day  while seeing the path to the deathless.
Better than living for a hundred years  without seeing the ultimate truth,  is living for one day  while seeing the ultimate truth.

Chapter of Evil
Rush to do good,  keep the mind back from evil.  One who is slow to do good  appreciates evil.
If a person does something evil  they should not do it again.  Take no interest in it;  the accumulation of evil is suffering.
If a person does something good  they should do it again.  Take an interest in it;  the accumulation of merit is pleasant.
One sees evil as good  as long as its results have yet to fully manifest;  but when the results of that evil fully manifest,  then one sees evil as evil.
One sees good as evil  as long as its results have yet to fully manifest;  but when the results of that good fully manifest,  then one sees good as good.
Do not disregard evil,  thinking it will have no consequence.  Just as falling drops of water  fill up a bucket,  a fool becomes full of evil  collecting it little by little.
Do not disregard merit,  thinking it will have no consequence.  Just as falling drops of water  fill up a bucket,  a sage becomes full of merit  collecting it little by little.
Just as a wealthy merchant with little protection  avoids a dangerous road,  just as one who wishes to live avoids poison,  one should avoid evil.
If a hand is unwounded  then it can take away poison;  poison cannot affect one who has no wound.  No evil comes to one who does none.
If one abuses  a faultless, pure, and flawless person,  then evil will come back to that fool,  like fine dust thrown against the wind.
Some people arise in wombs;  evildoers, in hell;  those on the right course go to heaven;  the uncorrupted attain Nibbāna.
Not by going into the sky, or into the ocean,  or into a mountain cleft,  or anywhere in the world,  can one find a place where one is free from one’s evil deeds.
Not by going into the sky, or into the ocean,  or into a mountain cleft,  or anywhere in the world,  can one find a place where one is not caught by death.

Chapter on Violence
Everyone dreads violence,  everyone fears death;  recognizing that you are similar,  do not harm or cause others to harm.
Everyone dreads violence,  everyone likes to live;  recognizing that you are similar,  do not harm or cause others to harm.
Beings want pleasure;  if one harms them with violence  while seeking pleasure for oneself,  one will find no pleasure in the future.
Beings want pleasure;  if one does not harm them with violence  while seeking pleasure for oneself,  one will find pleasure in the future.
Say no harsh words to anyone;  they might respond in kind.  Hostile speech is painful,  and it may provoke a violent response.
If you are non-reactive,  like a broken bell,  then you have reached Nibbāna  and no conflict can be found in you.
Just as a cowherd, using a stick,  herds cattle through a pasture,  in the same way, decrepitude and death  herd the living through life.
Performing evil actions,  a fool does not attain awakening.  The unwise person is tormented by those actions  as if burned by fire.
One who is violent towards the nonviolent,  one who harms the harmless,  will soon experience  one of ten consequences:
Harsh sensations, deprivation,  physical injury,  severe illness,  mental derangement,
legal trouble,  severe accusations,  loss of relatives,  dissipation of wealth,
or their house  catching on fire.  Then, when the fool is separated from their body,  they will reappear in hell.
Nudity, tangled hair, filth,  fasting, sleeping on the ground,  squatting in the mud -  these cannot purify a mortal who has not yet gone beyond doubt.

However, if one who wears adornments is well-behaved,  peaceful, restrained, committed to spiritual practice,  and has renounced violence towards all beings,  then they are a saint, a contemplative, a monk.
What person can be found in this world  that is restrained by conscience?  Who wakes up when criticized,  like a fine horse struck by a whip?

Like a fine horse struck by a whip,  be ardent and filled with urgency.  By means of faith, virtue, determination,  concentration, investigation of Dhamma,  perfect knowledge, perfect conduct, and thorough awareness,  abandon this immense suffering.
Irrigators guide water,  fletchers shape arrows,  carpenters shape wood,  those who practice well train themselves.

Chapter on Decay
Who can laugh, who can delight,  since this is always on fire?  Obscured by darkness,  you do not search for light.
See that the mind has been made a puppet,  damaged with arrogance,  afflicted with excessive thought,  lacking stability and composure.
This body is decrepit,  fragile, a nest of disease,  a putrid heap that falls apart,  since life ends in death.
Set aside  like gourds in autumn -  when seeing these faded bones,  what appreciation can there be?
Like a city made of bones,  wrapped in meat and blood,  a place of decay and death,  conceit and contempt.
Even splendid royal chariots wear out;  so too, this body decays.  But the true Dhamma never decays:  it is made known by those who are peaceful and virtuous.
A person who has learned little  ages like an ox:  their muscles grow  but their wisdom does not.
Wandering through many lives,  seeking but not finding  the builder of this house -  repeatedly experiencing the suffering of birth.

House-builder, you have been seen!  You will build no house again.  All your rafters are broken,  the roof-peak dismantled.  The mind has gone to the unconditioned -  the elimination of craving has been reached.
Those who have neither lived a spiritual life  nor acquired wealth during their youth,  Waste away like old herons  by a fishless pond.
Those who have neither lived a spiritual life  nor acquired wealth during their youth,  lay around like wasted arrows,  lamenting the past.

Chapter on Self
If one values oneself,  then one should guard oneself well;  during any of the three phases of the night,  a wise person should remain alert.
First one should settles oneself  in what is proper,  then one may instruct others;  a wise person should not become defiled.
One should act the same way  that one instructs others to act;  one who is well-trained can train others -  for it is truly hard to train oneself.
One is one’s own protector -  how could another protect you?  One who has trained oneself well  has acquired a protector that is truly hard to acquire.
Evil is done by oneself,  born from oneself, produced by oneself;  in this way a fool self-destructs,  like a diamond cutting through stone.
One who is excessively immoral,  like a tree overgrown by vines,  does to oneself  what an enemy wants.
It is easy to do things that are worthless  and of no benefit to oneself;  but to do what is beneficial and worthwhile  is extremely difficult.
A foolish person who,  based on a harmful perspective,  reviles the teachings  of the Worthy One,  brings about their own destruction  like a monocarpic plant.
By oneself evil is done,  by oneself one becomes defiled;  by oneself evil is not done,  by oneself one becomes purified;  purity and impurity depend on oneself -  no one can purify another.
One should not abandon one’s own welfare  for the sake of others, no matter how many;  having understood one’s own welfare,  one should be intent upon it.

Chapter of the World
One should not participate in inferior teachings,  one should not live negligently,  one should not participate in wrong view,  one should not increase worldliness.
One should apply effort, one should not be negligent,  one should practice Dhamma well;  one who practices the Dhamma rests happily,  in this world and the next.
One should practice Dhamma well,  one should not engage in misconduct;  one who practices the Dhamma rests happily,  in this world and the next.
Like seeing a bubble,  like seeing a mirage -  one who regards the world in this way  is not seen by the Lord of Death.
Come, look at this world,  as splendid as a royal chariot,  where fools become immersed,  but the conscious do not stick.
One who previously was negligent  but now is not  illuminates this world  like the moon set free from a cloud.
One who replaces their evil deeds  with wholesome ones  illuminates this world  like the moon set free from a cloud.
This world has become blind;  rare are those who see clearly.  Like a bird freed from a net,  few go to heaven.
Like swans moving through the air,  like mystics moving through the sky,  the wise leave this world,  having defeated Māra and his army.
There is no evil  that cannot be done  by one who tells lies  and disregards the afterlife.
Stingy fools, those who do not praise giving,  do not go the deva-world.  The wise rejoice in giving,  and because of that they are happy hereafter.
Compared to being the sole ruler of the earth,  or going to heaven,  or dominating the entire world,  attaining stream-entry is better.

Chapter on the Buddha
One whose victory does not diminish,  whose victory cannot be removed by anyone in the world,  the domain of that Awakened One is infinite -  No one can lead that one astray.
One who is not entangled or stuck,  in whom no craving can be found,  the domain of that Awakened One is infinite -  No one can lead that one astray.
They are steadfast, committed to Jhāna,  appreciate the peacefulness of renunciation,  and are envied even by the angels -  those who are mindful and fully Awakened.
It is hard to become a human,  it is hard to live a mortal life,  it is hard to hear the true Dhamma,  it is hard to encounter an Awakened One.
Not doing anything evil,  commitment to the wholesome,  and cleansing one's own mind -  this is the teaching of the Awakened Ones.
Endurance is the highest austerity,  Nibbāna is the highest, according to those who are Awakened.  A renunciant does not harm others,  a contemplative does not oppress others.

Not insulting, not harming,  self-restraint in accordance with the Pātimokkha,  Knowing the right amount when eating,  sitting and sleeping in a secluded place,  and commitment to improving the mind -  this is the teaching of the Awakened Ones.
Not even with a rain of money  can one be sated when it comes to sensuality.  There is little gratification in sensuality, it is unsatisfying;  this is what the wise understand.
Even in heavenly sensuality  one cannot find satisfaction.  But there is satisfaction in the elimination of craving  for a disciple of the Fully Awakened One.
They go to many places for refuge -  mountains, groves,  forest shrines -  people who are struck by fear.
But that is not a secure refuge,  that is not the ultimate refuge;  that is not a refuge  which brings freedom from all suffering.
But one who has gone for refuge  to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha,  and who sees the Four Noble Truths  with correct wisdom -
suffering, the origin of suffering,  the transcending of suffering,  and the Noble Eightfold Path  which leads to the pacification of suffering -
this is a secure refuge,  this is the ultimate refuge.  This is the refuge  which brings freedom from all suffering.
It is hard to find a high-quality person;  they are not born everywhere.  Wherever a steadfast person is born,  their family grows in happiness.
Happy is the arising of Awakened Ones,  happy is the teaching of the true Dhamma,  happy is the harmony of the Sangha,  happy is the austerity of those on the same Path.
One who honors those worthy of honor -  Awakened Ones or their disciples,  those who have transcended complication  and gone beyond sorrow and grief,
who have reached Nibbāna,  and are fearless -  it is not possible to calculate the merit  of one who honors such beings.

Chapter on Happiness
Oh so happily we live,  non-hostile amidst the hostile.  Amidst hostile people  we live without hostility.
Oh so happily we live,  unafflicted amidst the afflicted.  Amidst afflicted people  we live without affliction.
Oh so happily we live,  unpreoccupied amidst the preoccupied.  Amidst preoccupied people  we live without preoccupation.
Oh so happily we live,  we who have nothing.  We will feed on bliss,  like the radiant angels.
Victory produces hostility;  the defeated sleep uncomfortably.  The peaceful sleep happily,  having relinquished both victory and defeat.
There is no fire as strong as passion,  no distress as strong as aversion,  no suffering as strong as the components of being,  no happiness greater than peace
Hunger is the highest affliction,  conditions are the highest suffering;  for one who truly knows this,  Nibbāna is the highest happiness.
Freedom from illness is the highest acquisition,  contentment is the highest wealth,  trust is the highest kin,  Nibbāna is the highest happiness.
Having tasted the flavor of seclusion  and the flavor of peace,  free from anguish, flawless,  one tastes the bliss of the Dhamma.
It is good to see the Noble Ones,  living with them is always pleasant.  One who does not see fools  will always be happy.

Those who go with fools  will sorrow for a long time.  Living with fools is painful,  like being with an enemy all the time.  But living with the wise is pleasant,  like being together with one's relatives.
Therefore,  follow one who is steadfast, wise, and educated,  a good person who is patient, religious, noble, and astute,  follow that person,  as the moon follows the path of the stars.

The Preference Chapter

One who is dedicated to that which is not worthy of dedication,  and who is not dedicated to that which is worthy of dedication,  has dropped the goal and grabbed their preferences -  yet envies those who are intent upon self-development.
Don’t get caught up in what you prefer  or in what you do not prefer.  Not seeing what you prefer is hard to bear  and so is seeing what you do not prefer.
Therefore don’t form any preference;  loss of what one prefers is painful.  One who has no attachments  has no preferences.

One who is no longer attached to human existence,  and is not attached to celestial existence either;  one who is not attached to anything -  that is who I call a brahmin.
Having relinquished liking and disliking,  serene and non-possessive,  a hero who has overcome the entire world -  that is who I call a brahmin.
One who completely understands  the death and rebirth of sentient beings,  unattached, heavenly, awake -  that is who I call a brahmin.
One whose destiny is not known  by any angel, spirit, or human,  an Arahant whose corruptions have been eliminated -  that is who I call a brahmin.
One who has nothing before, after,  or in the middle;  one who is not possessive and not acquisitive -  that is who I call a brahmin.
A bull, an excellent hero,  a great sage, a victor,  unmoved, cleansed, awake -  that is who I call a brahmin.

One who knows their past lives,  who sees heaven and hell,  who has reached the elimination of birth,  a sage who has mastery of higher knowledge,  who has mastered every attainment -  that is who I call a brahmin.
Every Vice
Thus have I heard.  At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park.  There the Buddha addressed the monks:  “Monks!”
“Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.  The Buddha said this:
“Monks, I will teach you how to control every vice.  Listen to this and carefully apply your mind to it; I will speak.”
“Yes, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Buddha.  The Buddha said this:

“Monks, I say that the elimination of vices is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.  For one who knows and sees what?  Application of mind based on an understanding of causality, and application of mind not based on an understanding of causality.  Monks, when one applies one’s mind without an understanding of causality, one develops new vices, and one’s old vices grow stronger.  Monks, when one applies one’s mind based on an understanding of causality, one does not develop new vices, and one’s old vices are abandoned.

Monks, there are vices to be abandoned by seeing, vices to be abandoned by self-control, vices to be abandoned by using, vices to be abandoned by enduring, vices to be abandoned by avoiding, vices to be abandoned by removing, and vices to be abandoned by cultivating.
Vices to be Abandoned by Seeing

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by seeing?  In this case, monks, an uneducated commoner—one who does not see noble people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who does not see good people and is not skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people— does not understand what the mind should not be applied to and what the mind should be applied to.  Since they do not understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do not apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they apply their mind to?  Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger;  or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger;  or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger;  this is what the mind should not be applied to that they apply their mind to.

And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they do not apply their mind to?  Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned;  or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned;  or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned;  this is what the mind should be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.
So when they apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do not apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they develop new vices and their old vices grow stronger.

This is how they apply their mind without an understanding of causality:  they think, ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having done what, what did I become in the past?’  ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having done what, what will I become in the future?’  Or they are confused about the present:  ‘Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go from here?’

When one applies one’s mind in this way, one of six beliefs arises:  The belief ‘I have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.  Or the belief ‘I do not have a soul’ arises and seems true and certain.  Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.  Or the belief ‘Using the soul, I perceive what is not the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.  Or the belief ‘Using what is not the soul, I perceive the soul’ arises and seems true and certain.  Or they have this belief:  ‘This is my soul; it speaks, it feels, it experiences the results of good and evil actions; and this soul of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging, and will remain like this for eternity.’  Monks, this is called settling on a belief, becoming entangled in a belief, becoming disturbed by a belief, becoming agitated by a belief, becoming shackled by a belief.  Shackled by a belief, monks, the uneducated commoner is not freed from birth, decrepitude, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and anguish;  they are not freed from suffering, I say.

Monks, an educated disciple of the noble ones— one who sees noble people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of noble people, and who sees good people and is skilled and disciplined in the teachings of good people— understands what the mind the should be applied to and what the mind should not be applied to.  Since they understand what the mind should be applied and what the mind should not be applied to, they do not apply their mind to what they should not apply it to and they do apply their mind to what they should apply it to.

And, monks, what should the mind not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to?  Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, causes a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to grow stronger;  or causes a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to grow stronger;  or causes a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to grow stronger;  this is what the mind should not be applied to that they do not apply their mind to.

And, monks, what should the mind be applied to that they apply their mind to?  Monks, anything which, when the mind is applied to it, does not cause a new vice related to sensuality to develop, or causes an old vice related to sensuality to be abandoned;  or does not cause a new vice related to states of being to develop, or causes an old vice related to states of being to be abandoned;  or does not cause a new vice related to ignorance to develop, or causes an old vice related to ignorance to be abandoned;  this is what the mind should be applied to that they apply their mind to.

So when they do not apply their mind to that which it should not be applied to and do apply their mind to that which it should be applied to, they do not develop new vices and their old vices are abandoned.

They apply their mind based on an understanding of causality in this way: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the cause suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path of practice which leads to the cessation of suffering.’  Applying the mind based on an understanding of causality in this way, three shackles are abandoned:  belief in self-existence, skepticism, and misapprehension of habitual practices.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by seeing.
Vices to be Abandoned by Self-Control

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by self-control?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sight.  Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of sight, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of sight, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Contemplating causality, a monk practices self-control regarding the sense of sound…  sense of smell…  sense of taste…  sense of touch…  sense of cognition.  Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control regarding the sense of cognition, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.

Because, monks, when one does not practice self-control, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices self-control, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by self-control.
Vices to be Abandoned by Using

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by using?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk uses their robe  just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; and to cover the genitals.

Contemplating causality, a monk uses almsfood  not for entertainment, not for intoxication, not for beauty, not for decoration; but just for the sustenance and health of their body, and to support the spiritual life; thinking, ‘In this way, I will remove old feelings and I will not produce new feelings, so that I will be blameless and comfortable.’

Contemplating causality, a monk uses their dwelling  just for the purpose of not getting too cold; not getting too hot; not coming in contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; protection from weather; and to enjoy personal retreat.
Contemplating causality, a monk uses medicines and medicinal supplies  just for the purpose of preventing affliction and to be free from illness.

Because, monks, when one does not practice proper use, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one practices proper use, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by using.
Vices to be Abandoned by Enduring

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by enduring?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk endures cold and heat; hunger and thirst; contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles; improper and unwelcome statements; physical sensations that are painful, sharp, harsh, severe, uncomfortable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.

Because, monks, when one does not endure, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one endures, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by enduring.
Vices to be Abandoned by Avoiding

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by avoiding?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild ox, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, a thorn-bush, a pit, a precipice, a swamp, a sewer;  contemplating causality, a monk avoids sitting in improper places, going to improper places, or associating with evil friends, since such behavior might give one’s discerning spiritual companions cause for suspicion.

Because, monks, when one does not avoid such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one avoids such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by avoiding.
Vices to be Abandoned by Removing

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by removing?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk does not tolerate a sensual thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate an aversive thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate a malicious thought that is present, but instead abandons it, removes it, terminates it, and annihilates it; does not tolerate any harmful, unwholesome qualities that are present, but instead abandons them, removes them, terminates them, and annihilates them.

Because, monks, when one does not remove such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one removes such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by removing.
Vices to be Abandoned by Cultivating

Monks, what are the vices to be abandoned by cultivating?  In this case, monks, contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment;  contemplating causality, a monk cultivates the investigation factor of awakening…  the determination factor of awakening…  the euphoria factor of awakening…  the tranquility factor of awakening…  the concentration factor of awakening…  the equanimity factor of awakening, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and culminates in relinquishment;

Because, monks, when one does not cultivate such things, then disturbing and feverish vices develop; but when one cultivates such things, then those disturbing and feverish vices are not present.  Monks, these are called the vices to be abandoned by cultivating.

Monks, when a monk has abandoned by seeing the vices to be abandoned by seeing, has abandoned by self-control the vices to be abandoned by self-control, has abandoned by using the vices to be abandoned by using, has abandoned by enduring the vices to be abandoned by enduring, has abandoned by avoiding the vices to be abandoned by avoiding, has abandoned by removing the vices to be abandoned by removing, and has abandoned by cultivating the vices to be abandoned by cultivating,  that monk is called a monk who has controlled every vice, cut off craving, opened the shackles, and through a correct comprehension of conceit has put an end to suffering.”
This is what the Buddha said.  Satisfied, those monks rejoiced in the Buddha’s statement.
Stilling Thought
Thus have I heard.  At one time the Buddha was living at Sāvatthi, in Jeta’s grove, at Anāthapiṇḍika's park.  There the Buddha addressed the monks:  “Monks!”
“Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.  The Buddha said this:
“Monks, a monk who is committed to developing a heightened mind should regularly direct their mind in five ways.  What five?

In this case, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk should redirect their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, just as a skillful carpenter or apprentice carpenter could replace a coarse peg with a fine peg,  in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk should redirect their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts:  ‘These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts result in suffering.’  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, just as a young and well-adorned woman or man would be irritated, ashamed, and disgusted if the corpse of a snake, dog, or human was draped around their neck,  in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they redirect their mind, then they should examine the drawbacks of those thoughts:  ‘These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts result in suffering.’  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should not pay any attention to those thoughts.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, just as a person with eyes who did not want to see something in their field of view  could close their eyes or look away,  in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they examine the drawbacks of those thoughts, then by doing this those thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them, then they should direct the mind to stilling the production of those thoughts.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, just as a person who was moving quickly  might think,  ‘Why am I walking quickly?  I could walk slowly.’  So they walk slowly.  Then they think,  ‘Why am I walking slowly?  I could stand still.’  So they stand still.  Then they think,  ‘Why am I standing?  I could sit down.’  So they sit down.  Then they think,  ‘Why am I sitting?  I could lie down.’  So they lie down.  Monks, in this way that person gradually replaces coarse postures with more subtle ones.

in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they pay no attention to those thoughts, then by doing this those thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

Monks, if a monk does that, but evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, and delusion still arise in them,  then that monk should clench their teeth, press their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppress, overpower, and immobilize the mind.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, just as a strong person could grab a weaker person by the head, neck, or shoulders and suppress, overpower, and immobilize them,  in the same way, monks, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion continue to arise in a monk when they still the production of those thoughts,  then that monk should clench their teeth, press their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppress, overpower, and immobilize the mind.  When doing so, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.

Monks, when evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, aversion, or delusion arise in a monk while they are directing their mind towards something, then that monk redirects their mind to something that is connected with the wholesome, and those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  When one also examines the drawbacks of those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  When one also does not pay any attention to those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  When one also stills the production of those evil, unwholesome thoughts, then they are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  When one clenches their teeth, presses their tongue against the roof of their mouth, and mentally suppresses, overpowers, and immobilize the minds, then those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and come to an end.  Because they are abandoned, the mind becomes still, settled, unified, and collected.  Monks, this is called a monk that is in control of all the avenues of thought.  One will think whatever one wishes to think, and one will not think whatever one wishes to not think.  Craving will be cut off, the shackles will be opened, and through a correct comprehension of conceit suffering will be put to an end.”
This is what the Buddha said.  Satisfied, those monks rejoiced in the Buddha’s statement.
Sutta Nipāta
The Snake
A monk who removes anger when it appears,  as one removes a serpent’s venom using medicines,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who completely cuts off passion,  like a lotus plant dropping its flowers,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has completely severed craving,  who has dried up the swiftly flowing river,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who completely destroys conceit,  like a flood destroys a fragile bamboo bridge,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who sees no value in states of being,  as one does not find flowers on fig trees,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk in whom there is no anger,  who has completely gone beyond both being and non-being,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has completely blown away their thoughts,  whose mind is internally well-ordered,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who transcends all this complication,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who knows that the world is completely false,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who is free of greed, knowing it to be completely false,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who is free of passion, knowing it to be completely false,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who is free of hatred, knowing it to be completely false,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who neither goes too far nor goes back,  who is free of delusion, knowing it to be completely false,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has no subconscious tendencies,  who has eliminated the unwholesome roots,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has no anxiety whatsoever  about this life or the next,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has no desire whatsoever  based on which one might be bound to existence,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
A monk who has discarded the five hindrances,  who is untroubled, free of doubt, unafflicted,  relinquishes both the here and the beyond  like a snake shedding its decayed skin.
Sutta Nipāta
Discourse to Dhaniya

“I have prepared cooked rice and fresh milk,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “I stay constantly at the shore of the great river,  “I have a closed hut with a fire kindled;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“I have no anger and no corruption,”  said the Buddha,  “I stay one night at the shore of the great river,  “I have an open hut with the fire extinguished;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“There are no gadflies or mosquitoes,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “In the marshes and meadows where the cattle roam,  “When it rained in the past, they could endure;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“The raft was assembled and well-contructed,”  said the Buddha,  “It crossed over to the far shore, it went past the deluge;  “I have no need of a raft;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“My cowherd-woman listens and is prudent,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “For a long time, she has been a pleasant co-resident,  “I have never heard anything evil from her;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“My mind is unpolluted and liberated,”  said the Buddha,  “For a long time, it has been thoroughly developed and well-trained,  “No evil can be found in me;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“I have a servant that I hired myself,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “My children are all equally healthy,  “I have never heard anything evil from them;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”
“I am not the servant of anyone,”  said the Buddha,  “I travel the entire world with what I have gained,  “I have no need of wages;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”
“There is a cow and a suckling calf,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “There is the herd-mother with her offspring,  “The father-bull as well;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”
“There is no cow and no suckling calf,”  said the Buddha,  “No herd-mother and no offspring,  “And no father-bull as well;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”

“The post is firmly entrenched and does not wobble,”  said Dhaniya the Cowherd,  “The ropes are made of new and well-made twine,  “It is not possible for the calves to break them;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”
“Like a bull that has broken its bonds,”  said the Buddha,  “Like an elephant that has burst through rotten vines,  “I will never again enter a womb;  “So if the angels wish, they can make it rain.”
Flooding both the low ground and the high ground,  a great raincloud poured down rain.  After hearing the rain from the angels,  Dhaniya spoke about this:
“It is a gain for us, and not a small one,  “That we have seen the Buddha;  “I take refuge in the Seer,  “Great Sage, be our teacher.
“I am a cow-herd, and I listen,  “I will live the spiritual life following the Sublime One,  “To go beyond birth and death,  “And bring suffering to an end.”

“One who has children delights because of their children,”  said Māra the Evil One,  “One who has cattle delights because of their cattle,  “Possessions are the delight of a person,  “One who has no possessions has no delight.”

“One who has children sorrows because of their children,”  said the Buddha,  “One who has cattle sorrows because of their cattle,  “Possessions are the the sorrow of a person,  “One who has no possessions has no sorrow.”
